title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
hook: he turns toward Jerusalem; foxes have holes, but he has nowhere to lay his head

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child set beside Jesus while the disciples argued about rank. Your line was the least is the greatest. Whose need did you put first? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Here, halfway through chapter nine, Luke's Gospel turns a corner, and you can almost feel the road tilt. In the King James words: "when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." For the next ten chapters, Jesus is walking. Every story from here on, the Good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus in the tree, happens on the road to Jerusalem, the city where he knows what's waiting. Set his face. It's a picture from the prophet Isaiah, where God's servant says: "therefore have I set my face like a flint." Flint. Hard stone. Not stubbornness. Resolve.

The road goes through Samaria first. Samaritans and Jews had a long, bitter history, with old disputes over the right place to worship. Jesus sends messengers ahead to find a place to stay, and a Samaritan village turns them away, Luke says, because he was heading to Jerusalem. James and John are furious: "Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?" Fire from heaven, like Elijah. And Luke says: "he turned, and rebuked them." They simply go to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you anywhere. Jesus answers: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Anywhere includes nowhere. The second, Jesus invites: follow me. The man says, let me first go and bury my father. And Jesus says something startling: "Let the dead bury their dead." Scholars still debate what this meant: whether the father had already died, or whether the man meant waiting until his father was old and gone someday. The text doesn't say. What's clear is the urgency. The third says, let me first say goodbye to my family. And Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." Anyone who has plowed knows: look back over your shoulder and the furrow goes crooked. You keep your eyes on a point ahead, and you walk toward it.
screen: `HAND TO THE PLOUGH, NO LOOKING BACK.`
then, large: `HE STEDFASTLY SET HIS FACE TO GO TO JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set your face toward one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Everyone has something they keep circling and not doing. A hard conversation. A doctor's appointment. A debt to face, an apology to make, a job application, a habit to end. Let yours come up. Notice how you usually look back: the excuses, the let-me-first, the someday. Now picture a plowman with a point fixed on the far side of the field. Picture your face set toward your hard thing, calm, steady, flint, not angry. Choose the very first step, the one you could take today. If you pray, you can ask for a steady face. If you don't, simply fix your eyes on the step. The bell holds the time.
He set his face. Luke's turning point: Jesus resolves to go to Jerusalem, rebukes the call for fire, and tells would-be followers not to look back from the plow.
Your line: no looking back. Take the first step toward your hard thing today, and when the let-me-first voices start, keep your eyes on the point ahead. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians call Luke 9:51 to 19:28 the travel narrative, and some churches read through it slowly as a journey toward Holy Week.

original.note: Greek: he set firm his face. an echo of the old Greek Bible's way of saying a face fixed toward something.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was being stubborn.
what it means: he chooses, calmly, to walk toward Jerusalem and what waits there, and asks his followers not to keep looking back.
what a scholar hears: "set his face" echoes Isaiah 50:7, "I set my face like a flint," and begins Luke's long travel narrative, 9:51 to 19:28.
